h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in St. Louis
intro:
St. Louis is a brick city, and that single fact shapes almost every renovation budget here. Solid masonry walls, soft handmade brick, lime mortar, flat roofs behind parapets and two-family flats stacked one above the other make the work different from a frame-house market. Investors who price St. Louis rehabs like suburban jobs tend to miss the tuckpointing, the box gutters and the occupancy inspection.

Genstone Construction renovates investment property in St. Louis for individual investors, funds, banks, servicers and Government-Sponsored Enterprises. We are based in Romeoville, Illinois, and in St. Louis we coordinate licensed, insured local contractors who work on this housing stock every day, with one designated field manager answering to you. The process opens with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review that prices repairs and tests your after-repair value before you commit. You then receive a written scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule. Permits, inspections and lien waivers are handled, nothing is paid upfront, and dumpster and debris removal are already in the number.
housingStock:
Much of the city’s character traces back to the aftermath of the Great Fire of 1849, when St. Louis moved toward brick and stone construction, and to the clay deposits that let local brickyards supply that brick in enormous volume. The result is a housing stock where masonry is the default, not the upgrade.

Near downtown and the river, Soulard, Lafayette Square and Benton Park hold Federal-style and Second Empire rowhouses and shotgun cottages from the mid to late 1800s, many with mansard roofs clad in slate, shared party walls and narrow lots with alley access. Lafayette Square and Soulard are locally designated historic districts, so exterior work goes through additional review.

Moving south and west, Tower Grove East, Tower Grove South, Shaw, Fox Park and Dutchtown are dense with the classic St. Louis flat: a two-family building with one unit stacked over the other, along with four-family flats and corner storefronts with apartments above. Bevo Mill and Holly Hills mix flats with brick bungalows, and St. Louis Hills and Princeton Heights carry well-built 1920s through 1940s brick bungalows, cottages and some early ranches.

North St. Louis has some of the oldest and most ornate brick housing in the city, in neighborhoods such as Hyde Park, College Hill and the Ville, alongside widespread vacancy. Vacant buildings there have suffered from brick theft, where salvagers pull walls apart for resale, leaving structures that are unsafe.

What this means for a rehab: plan for tuckpointing with the correct soft mortar, inspect parapets and chimneys, expect flat or low-slope roofs with internal box gutters on flats, and assume original galvanized and cast-iron plumbing, knob-and-tube remnants and lead paint until shown otherwise. Plaster on masonry walls behaves differently from plaster on studs, and insulating exterior walls is rarely practical.

commonIssues.title: Tuckpointing and the wrong mortar
commonIssues.body: Soft St. Louis brick was laid in lime mortar that is meant to wear before the brick does. When someone repoints with hard Portland cement mortar, the brick faces start to spall and pop off instead. We see this constantly on south city flats. A proper repointing job uses a compatible mortar, and on badly damaged walls it may require replacing individual bricks with salvaged matches. We assess masonry closely because it is one of the largest exterior costs on a St. Louis purchase.

commonIssues.title: Flat roofs, parapets and box gutters
commonIssues.body: Most St. Louis flats have a low-slope roof hidden behind a parapet, draining to an internal box gutter or scupper. When the flashing at the parapet fails or the box gutter liner rusts through, water runs into the masonry and down into the top-floor unit. Leaks often appear far from their source. We inspect parapet caps, coping, flashings and gutter liners, and we price roof replacement with the parapet repairs included rather than discovering them mid-job.

commonIssues.title: Cast-iron stacks and old laterals
commonIssues.body: Original plumbing in St. Louis houses typically means cast-iron drain stacks, galvanized supply lines and old clay or cast-iron sewer laterals running to the alley or street. Stacks crack along their seams, galvanized lines restrict flow and rust, and laterals collapse or fill with roots. Flats add complexity because both units often share one stack. We recommend a camera inspection before closing and price stack replacement through both floors as a single, coordinated item.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint everywhere
commonIssues.body: With most of the housing built long before 1978, lead-based paint is nearly universal in St. Louis rehab work, on window sashes, trim, porches and exterior masonry coatings. Renovation, repair and painting rules apply to any work that disturbs it, and rental properties face additional scrutiny. We plan lead-safe work practices, containment and cleaning into the scope and use certified firms where needed, which also protects your position if a tenant or buyer raises lead concerns later.

commonIssues.title: Structural damage in vacant buildings
commonIssues.body: Long-vacant St. Louis buildings, especially on the north side, can have collapsed roofs, rotted joists, missing brick from salvage theft and fire damage. Water entering through an open roof destroys floor framing fast. Some of these buildings can be saved with shoring, new joists and rebuilt walls, while others are condemned. We evaluate structural condition carefully during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, and when a structural engineer is needed, we coordinate that review before you commit funds.

investorMarket:
St. Louis investors tend to sort themselves by neighborhood and building type, and the strategy that works on one side of Grand Boulevard can fail on the other.

Flips perform where owner-occupant demand is steady: Tower Grove South, Shaw, Southampton, St. Louis Hills, Princeton Heights, Holly Hills and parts of Bevo Mill. Buyers there want character, so refinished hardwood, exposed brick and original trim can carry real value when the systems behind them are new.

Two-family flats are the backbone of the city’s small-landlord market. Many investors buy flats in Dutchtown, Gravois Park, Mount Pleasant, Bevo Mill and Tower Grove East, live in one unit or rent both, and rely on the second unit to cover a large share of the payment. Some flats are later converted back into single-family homes in stronger neighborhoods, which is a legitimate flip strategy of its own.

BRRRR and buy-and-hold rentals work across south city and in some north city pockets, but north side investing requires extra care around structural condition, vacancy and comparable sales. The Land Reutilization Authority holds a large inventory of city-owned property, and many investors buy through it.

Just past the city line, St. Louis County’s municipalities such as Affton, Maplewood and Florissant offer frame and brick ranches and bungalows, but many of those municipalities require point-of-sale or occupancy inspections, which affect your scope and closing timeline.
permits:
Building permits in the City of St. Louis are issued by the Building Division, which sits within the Department of Public Safety. Structural work, additions, roofing, new electrical, plumbing and mechanical work, and significant remodeling all need permits, with inspections at the rough-in and final stages. Licensed trade contractors pull the electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits.

Two local requirements matter a great deal to investors. First, the city requires occupancy permits and inspections for many residential units when new occupants move in, so a rental or a resale needs to meet those standards before someone can legally take possession. Second, the Cultural Resources Office reviews exterior work in locally designated historic districts, including Soulard and Lafayette Square, and that review covers items such as windows, doors, roofing materials and masonry.

Outside the city limits, each St. Louis County municipality runs its own permitting and many conduct point-of-sale inspections. Genstone prepares applications, schedules inspections, collects lien waivers and tracks occupancy requirements so the property can be leased or sold on schedule.
climate:
St. Louis summers are hot and very humid, and winters swing between mild spells and hard freezes. That freeze-thaw pattern is hard on masonry: water that soaks into soft brick and failed mortar expands when it freezes, which is how parapets, chimneys and porch steps deteriorate.

Spring and summer storms bring heavy rain, hail and the occasional tornado warning. Intense downpours overwhelm box gutters and old downspouts, and basements in older houses take on water when grading and drainage have been neglected. Humid air in an unconditioned vacant building encourages mold within a season.

We schedule tuckpointing, masonry and roofing for temperatures that allow mortar and sealants to cure, keep vacant houses heated or winterized through cold months, and put air conditioning in early on summer jobs so finishing trades can work in a dry building.

faqs.q: Does Genstone have a St. Louis office?
faqs.a: No. Our headquarters is in Romeoville, Illinois. In St. Louis we coordinate vetted, licensed and insured contractors who know brick construction, flats and the city’s occupancy process, all managed by one designated field manager. You get a single point of contact, a written scope and draw schedule, and documented progress without needing to manage individual trades yourself. This approach also lets us cover St. Louis County municipalities and the Metro East.

faqs.q: Do you work on two-family flats?
faqs.a: Yes, flats are one of the most common building types we see in St. Louis. We renovate them as two-unit rentals, convert them for owner-occupant house hacking, and in some cases scope a conversion back to a single-family home. Each approach has different implications for utilities, egress, permits and the eventual buyer, and we lay those out during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review.

faqs.q: Can you help with occupancy inspections?
faqs.a: Yes. We scope work so a property is ready for the City of St. Louis occupancy inspection and for point-of-sale or occupancy inspections in St. Louis County municipalities. Common items include smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, handrails, electrical hazards, plumbing leaks, broken windows and peeling paint. Addressing them during the renovation avoids failed inspections and delays in leasing or selling the property.

faqs.q: How do you price masonry work before I buy?
faqs.a: During the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review we walk the exterior closely, looking at parapets, chimneys, mortar joints, lintels, sills and any spalled or missing brick. We price tuckpointing with compatible mortar, rebuilding where needed and any structural items as separate lines. On St. Louis brick buildings, this is often the single largest exterior cost, so it should be part of your offer math.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in St. Louis, MO | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: St. Louis flip renovations for brick bungalows, flats and rowhouses: masonry-first scopes, character-preserving finishes and occupancy-ready work.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in St. Louis
fix-flip.intro: The St. Louis flip buyer is shopping for brick, hardwood and character with modern systems behind it. They will walk through a Tower Grove South bungalow or a converted Shaw flat looking at exposed brick and original trim, and their inspector will be looking at the parapet, the mortar and the electrical panel. Genstone Construction plans flips that satisfy both. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the hidden masonry and plumbing items and refines your after-repair value against renovated comps, and the scope we write often includes two finish levels so you can compare margin. A designated field manager runs the work with licensed local trades, permits and the city’s occupancy inspection are handled, and draws follow completed work with no upfront payment required.

sections.h2: Where St. Louis flips sell and what buyers expect
sections.body:
St. Louis flip demand concentrates in south city neighborhoods with strong owner-occupant traffic: Tower Grove South, Shaw, Southampton, St. Louis Hills, Princeton Heights, Holly Hills and the better blocks of Bevo Mill. Buyers there are often coming from apartments or from the county and want city character without old-house headaches.

That means finishes should respect the building. Refinished original oak or pine floors, restored trim where it survives, and exposed brick on an interior wall tend to photograph and show well. Kitchens and baths should be fully modern, and buyers notice when a renovation looks cheap against original plaster and woodwork.

In Soulard, Lafayette Square and Benton Park, rowhouse buyers expect a higher level of finish and historically sensitive exterior work, and the Cultural Resources Office has its own say about the facade. We write each scope against the comps you are using and flag where a finish upgrade is unlikely to return its cost.

sections.h2: Masonry, roof and plumbing before paint
sections.body:
In St. Louis, the expensive surprises sit above the ceiling and inside the walls. A flip that skips the parapet, the box gutter or the drain stack is likely to be renegotiated after the buyer’s inspection. We price those items first and treat cosmetics as what is left after the building is sound.

That usually means repointing with a lime-compatible mortar wherever joints have failed, rebuilding loose parapet sections and chimney tops, replacing the low-slope roof with properly flashed edges, and relining or replacing box gutters. Inside, we plan to replace galvanized supply lines and cracked cast-iron stacks, camera the lateral and update electrical service and wiring.

On bungalows in St. Louis Hills and Princeton Heights, the masonry is usually in better shape, but original wiring, aging boilers and basement water problems still appear. The goal is a house where the buyer’s inspector finds very little to write about, which protects your sale price and your closing date.

sections.h2: Occupancy inspection and the closing timeline
sections.body:
Selling a house in the City of St. Louis often involves an occupancy inspection before the new owner can move in, and many St. Louis County municipalities run their own point-of-sale inspections. A failed inspection can delay closing and add carrying costs, so we build the likely checklist into the flip scope from the beginning.

Typical items include smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in the right places, secure handrails and guardrails, GFCI protection, working windows, no exposed wiring, no plumbing leaks and intact paint. We schedule the inspection as the job finishes and correct any item that comes back.

Permits matter for resale too. Buyers’ agents and appraisers increasingly ask whether electrical, plumbing and mechanical work was permitted, and the Building Division’s records show it. Our field manager keeps permits current and closed so the house is ready to list as soon as the last trade leaves. Open permits found at closing are an avoidable delay.

faqs.q: Should I flip a two-family flat as a single-family home?
faqs.a: Sometimes. In neighborhoods such as Tower Grove South and Shaw, converting a flat back to one house can produce a larger, more valuable home for owner-occupant buyers. Elsewhere, buyers who want rental income may pay more for a renovated two-unit building. We help you test both approaches with the comps during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review before deciding which way to go.

faqs.q: Do historic district rules affect my St. Louis flip?
faqs.a: If the house is in a locally designated historic district such as Soulard or Lafayette Square, exterior changes go through review by the Cultural Resources Office. That can affect windows, doors, roofing materials and masonry repairs. We factor those requirements into the scope and timeline so approvals are obtained before exterior work begins and the sale is not held up.

faqs.q: How do you handle lead paint on a flip?
faqs.a: Nearly every St. Louis house we flip was built before 1978, so we plan lead-safe work practices for any task that disturbs painted surfaces. That includes containment, proper cleanup and using certified firms where required. It protects workers, future occupants and you, and it means the house can be marketed without lead hazards left behind on windows, trim or porches.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in St. Louis, MO | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR renovations in St. Louis built for the refinance appraisal and long holds: masonry, roofs, stacks and occupancy-ready units in brick buildings.
brrrr.intro: St. Louis has been a BRRRR market for years because brick houses and flats can still be bought at prices that leave room for a full renovation. The plan only works, though, if the refinance appraisal lands where you need it and the building does not punish you with roof leaks and stack failures during the hold. Genstone Construction scopes BRRRR projects in St. Louis with both outcomes in mind. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review tests the likely appraisal against renovated sales and prices the masonry, roofing and plumbing work that protects your cash flow. A designated field manager coordinates licensed local trades, permits and the city’s occupancy inspection are handled, and draws follow completed work. Genstone Financial’s DSCR rental loans can support the refinance stage when you are ready.

sections.h2: Reading St. Louis comps for the refinance
sections.body:
Appraisals in St. Louis can vary sharply from one block to the next. A renovated house in Tower Grove South might sit a few streets from blocks where few properties have sold in years. For BRRRR investors in Dutchtown, Gravois Park, Mount Pleasant, Bevo Mill and parts of north city, the refinance value is the number most likely to break the plan.

Before you buy, we look at which renovated houses and flats an appraiser is likely to use, how recently they sold and what condition they were in. Then we scope your renovation to match or exceed them in the items appraisers count: updated kitchens and baths, new mechanicals, roof condition and functional space.

On flats, an appraiser may value the building on income as well as sales. A clean, legal, fully rentable second unit with its own utilities supports that analysis far better than an outdated unit that only looks rentable in photographs.

sections.h2: Building for a long hold in brick
sections.body:
Once your refinance closes, the maintenance profile of a St. Louis brick building matters more than its finishes. Roofs, parapets and box gutters cause more damage over a hold period than anything else, because water entering at the top finds its way through masonry and plaster before anyone notices.

We prioritize roof and parapet work, tuckpointing where water is getting in, and drainage away from the foundation. Inside, we replace galvanized supply lines and cracked cast-iron stacks so you are not opening finished walls later. Older boilers and gravity furnaces are evaluated for replacement, and we add central air where the building can accept it, since St. Louis summers make cooling a tenant expectation.

Finishes are chosen to survive turnover: luxury vinyl plank or refinished hardwood, scrubbable paint, durable counters and fixtures with available parts. That way, each turnover during your hold is a cleaning and touch-up job rather than another renovation.

sections.h2: Passing the St. Louis occupancy inspection
sections.body:
Before a new tenant moves into many city rental units, St. Louis requires an occupancy permit and inspection. Plan for it in your BRRRR schedule; a failed inspection means a unit that cannot be legally occupied, which delays the rent your refinance depends on.

We scope each unit with the inspector’s checklist in mind: working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, safe electrical with no open junctions or exposed wiring, secure handrails, functional heat, working windows and locks, no leaks and intact paint surfaces. In pre-1978 buildings, paint condition is examined closely because of lead.

Our field manager schedules the inspection as work finishes and handles corrections quickly. When your BRRRR property is a flat with two units, each unit is prepared to pass on its own, so one unfinished unit does not hold up the other from producing income.

County properties follow different rules. A BRRRR house in Florissant or Affton answers to that municipality’s inspection program instead, and we confirm the checklist for each address before writing the scope.

faqs.q: Are flats good BRRRR candidates in St. Louis?
faqs.a: Often. Two-family flats can offer strong rent relative to purchase price, and a renovated building with separate utilities is attractive to lenders and tenants alike. The risks are the shared roof, stack and masonry, which can be expensive. We price those building-wide items clearly during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you can judge the full project cost before the appraisal question even comes up.

faqs.q: Can you provide documentation for the appraiser?
faqs.a: Yes. We provide the scope, before and after photographs, permit records and lien waivers. In St. Louis, where comps can be thin and appraisers may not see behind walls, a clear record of new roofing, plumbing, electrical and mechanical work helps support the value. That package also helps when you work with Genstone Financial on a DSCR refinance, since the lender sees the same records.

faqs.q: Do you work on north St. Louis BRRRR projects?
faqs.a: Yes, with a careful look at structure, vacancy and comparable sales first. Many north city buildings have strong bones but long periods of vacancy, water damage or missing brick from salvage theft. We evaluate whether the building can be saved economically and whether the refinance value supports the plan before recommending you move forward. Sometimes the honest answer is to pass on a building.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in St. Louis, MO | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: St. Louis single-family rental renovations and turns: brick-building durability, occupancy inspection readiness, portfolio standards, field manager.
rental-renovation.h1: Rental Property Renovations in St. Louis
rental-renovation.intro: St. Louis single-family rentals range from brick bungalows in Princeton Heights to frame ranches just over the line in Affton and Florissant. Owners range from one-house landlords to funds holding scattered portfolios. All of them need renovations and turns that survive tenants, satisfy occupancy inspectors and keep vacancy short. Genstone Construction handles rental renovations and turns across the city and surrounding county municipalities with a designated field manager and licensed local contractors. Each scope lays out labor, materials and a draw schedule, permits are pulled where needed, and every job is documented with photos so you can manage it from anywhere. Through Genstone Field Services, we also coordinate make-ready work, inspections and occupied maintenance between tenancies.

sections.h2: A rental standard that fits St. Louis houses
sections.body:
A written rental standard keeps costs predictable: one flooring product, one paint palette, the same fixture and appliance package across every property. For St. Louis portfolios, the standard also has to account for the building type.

Brick bungalows in St. Louis Hills, Princeton Heights and Holly Hills usually have plaster walls, hardwood floors worth keeping and basements that need to stay dry rather than finished. Frame ranches in the county suburbs often have drywall, slab or crawlspace foundations and more straightforward mechanical layouts. A good standard adapts to each without letting quality drift.

We help portfolio owners define that standard and then apply it consistently. When a house needs work outside the standard, such as tuckpointing, a new stack or a roof, we price it as a separate line so you can see what the asset needs beyond a normal turn and plan capital spending accordingly. Over a few years, that record shows which houses earn their keep.

sections.h2: Turnover work that lasts in St. Louis
sections.body:
Rental turns in St. Louis are a chance to fix the problems that cause midlease calls. We look at gutters and downspouts, roof edges and window glazing alongside the interior checklist, because water entering through the masonry or windows is the most common source of damage in older brick houses.

Inside, we repair plaster or drywall, repaint with scrubbable finishes, replace worn carpet with luxury vinyl plank, re-caulk wet areas and service the furnace or boiler and air conditioning. Original hardwood is often worth refinishing rather than covering, since it holds up well and tenants value it.

We document tenant damage separately from normal wear, with photographs, so deposit decisions are supported. Turns are scheduled to minimize vacant days and to keep heat on through the winter months, when frozen supply lines in exterior masonry walls become a real risk in an empty house. Summer turns get the air conditioning checked first.

Many City of St. Louis rentals require an occupancy inspection when a new tenant moves in, and county municipalities such as Florissant, Maplewood and University City have their own occupancy or rental inspection programs. A failed inspection holds up move-in and rent.

We scope turns to pass on the first visit: smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, safe electrical, secure stairs and rails, working windows, functional heat and plumbing, and intact paint, which matters for lead in older houses. Our field manager schedules the inspection and handles any corrections the same week whenever possible.

For tenants already in place, Genstone Field Services coordinates occupied maintenance: scheduling access, protecting belongings and completing repairs efficiently. A documented record of what was done and when also helps if a tenant disputes the condition of the home or a city inspector follows up on a complaint. Those records stay attached to the property file for as long as you own the house.

faqs.q: Do you handle rental turns in St. Louis County?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate licensed contractors across the city and county municipalities such as Affton, Maplewood, Florissant and University City. Since many of those municipalities run their own occupancy or rental inspection programs, we confirm the requirements for each address and scope the turn to meet them. Portfolio owners get consistent pricing and documentation across both city and county properties, managed by one field manager.

faqs.q: Should I keep the hardwood floors in my rentals?
faqs.a: In many St. Louis brick bungalows and flats, yes. Original oak or pine floors are durable, appeal to tenants and can be refinished several times. Where floors are badly damaged or in wet areas, luxury vinyl plank is a better choice. We assess condition during the turn and recommend the option with the better long-term cost for that particular house.

faqs.q: Is there a warranty on rental work?
faqs.a: Our St. Louis rental work comes with a one-year workmanship warranty. Damage caused by tenants, and ordinary wear over time, fall outside that coverage. If an item we installed fails due to workmanship within that year, we return to correct it. Our documentation of each job makes it easy to confirm what was installed and when, which keeps warranty conversations short and factual for everyone involved.

multifamily-renovation.title: Two-Family Flat Renovation in St. Louis, MO | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: St. Louis two-family and four-family flat renovations: stacked units, shared stacks and roofs, utility separation, occupied phasing and permits.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Two-Family and Four-Family Flat Renovations in St. Louis
multifamily-renovation.intro: The St. Louis flat is one of the most recognizable small multifamily buildings in the country: a brick building with one apartment stacked over another, or four units arranged two up and two down, often with a separate entrance for each. South city neighborhoods such as Tower Grove East, Dutchtown, Bevo Mill and Gravois Park are full of them. They make excellent rentals when renovated well, but they share roofs, stacks, masonry and sometimes heat. Genstone Construction renovates flats with scopes broken out by unit and by building-wide system, phasing work around tenants when needed. One field manager runs the job with licensed local trades, permits and occupancy inspections are handled, and draws are tied to completed work with no upfront payment.

sections.h2: How St. Louis flats are built
sections.body:
Most St. Louis flats are solid masonry buildings with interior bearing walls, a low-slope roof behind a parapet, and a full basement holding the mechanical equipment for both units. The upper unit usually reaches its door through a separate front entrance and an interior stair, with a rear porch or exterior stair providing a second exit.

This layout creates predictable renovation priorities. The roof and parapet protect both units, so failures there damage the upper unit first and then the lower. Plumbing stacks run through both apartments, so replacing a cracked cast-iron stack means opening walls in each. Rear porches and stairs, often wood, are frequently the most deteriorated part of the building and serve as the required second exit for the upper unit.

We write flat scopes with building-wide items separated from unit interiors so you can see the true cost of the shell and plan accordingly. Lenders and partners usually want that split too.

Many older flats were built with separate meters, but some were later combined onto a single boiler or electrical service, and four-family buildings in particular may share heat. Separating utilities lets each tenant pay their own costs, which improves income and makes the building easier to finance.

Separating heat often means replacing an old shared boiler with individual furnaces and new ductwork, which in masonry buildings requires careful planning for duct routes and venting. Electrical work may include new services and panels for each unit. We price these as distinct line items so you can decide whether the rent difference justifies the investment.

Adding central air is another common upgrade in St. Louis flats, where summers are hot and humid. In upper units, high-velocity or ductless systems can avoid tearing into plaster ceilings. We look at each building’s layout before recommending a system so the result is practical and efficient.

Buying a St. Louis flat with one unit occupied is common. We phase work so the vacant unit is completed first, then turn to the occupied unit once the lease ends or the tenant moves into the finished apartment. Building-wide items such as roof replacement, tuckpointing and stack replacement are scheduled with advance notice to tenants and with water and power shutoffs kept as short as possible.

The city’s occupancy inspection applies when new tenants move in, so each unit is prepared to pass independently. Exterior masonry and roofing work is planned for weather that allows mortar and roofing materials to set properly, while interior work in the vacant unit continues regardless.

Your field manager coordinates tenant access, keeps common areas safe and clean, and posts progress so you can report to partners or lenders without walking the building yourself. Tenants also get a named contact for questions during the work.

faqs.q: Can I convert a four-family flat into a two-family?
faqs.a: Often, yes, and in some neighborhoods it produces larger units that rent faster and attract longer-term tenants. Conversions require permits and may involve zoning review, along with new kitchens, baths and egress planning. We evaluate the layout during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and outline what the conversion would take before you decide whether to pursue it. Utility separation is often part of that plan.

faqs.q: Who pays for the shared roof and stack work?
faqs.a: As the owner of the whole building, you do, but we break those costs out separately from unit interiors so you can see exactly what the shell requires. That helps with underwriting, especially when a lender or partner wants to understand the capital needs of the building beyond cosmetic updates to each apartment. It also shows which costs recur and which are one-time.

faqs.q: Do you rebuild rear porches and stairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Rear porches on St. Louis flats often serve as the second exit for upper units and are frequently in poor condition. We assess framing, footings and railings, pull permits, and rebuild to current requirements. That improves safety and helps the building pass occupancy inspections when new tenants move in. Treated lumber, proper footings and sound ledger connections extend their life considerably.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203k Contractor in St. Louis, MO | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor serving St. Louis buyers, agents and lenders: bids for brick homes and flats, consultant coordination and draws.
fha-203k.intro: In St. Louis, FHA 203(k) loans let buyers purchase solid brick houses and two-family flats that need work and finance the renovation in the same loan. That is a natural fit for a city where many of the most attractive homes need roofs, tuckpointing and new systems before they are comfortable. Genstone carries FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor status for exactly this kind of work. We provide itemized bids, coordinate with the HUD consultant on Standard loans, handle permits and occupancy inspections, and submit draw requests with photos and lien waivers. Buyers get one designated field manager, agents get a contractor who understands the process, and lenders receive documentation in the form they expect at every draw.

sections.h2: Choosing the right 203(k) for a St. Louis home
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) is designed for non-structural repairs up to $75,000, which suits many south city bungalows that need new mechanicals, a roof, updated kitchens and baths, and paint and flooring. The Standard 203(k) covers structural repairs and larger scopes and requires a HUD-approved consultant. Genstone’s program materials note a $5,000 minimum and a $15,000 inspection threshold.

In St. Louis, the dividing line is often masonry. Rebuilding a parapet, replacing a failed lintel, repairing a bowed basement wall or reframing floors damaged by a roof leak can count as structural work and push the project to a Standard loan. We evaluate the house with that in mind during our review, so buyers and loan officers start on the right path rather than switching programs partway through.

Roof and box gutter condition is the other early question. A flat roof that needs full replacement with parapet flashing and new gutter liners is a substantial line, and it has to fit inside the loan alongside the interior work the buyer actually wants.

sections.h2: St. Louis properties that fit the program
sections.body:
Good St. Louis 203(k) candidates include brick bungalows in St. Louis Hills, Princeton Heights, Holly Hills and Bevo Mill that are structurally sound but need systems and finishes, and two-family flats where an owner-occupant plans to live in one unit and rent the other. FHA allows financing of two-to-four unit properties when the buyer occupies one unit, which makes flats especially popular with 203(k) buyers.

Larger rowhouses in Soulard or Lafayette Square can also work, though historic district review and higher costs need to fit within loan limits. Long-vacant north city buildings with structural damage are harder; the scope and appraised value must line up. We help buyers, agents and lenders see early whether a specific property fits the program so time is not wasted on a house that cannot close.

County homes are candidates too. Brick and frame ranches in Affton and Florissant often need only mechanicals, a roof and cosmetic updates, which keeps them comfortably within a Limited loan, though their municipal occupancy inspections still need to be planned into the bid.

A 203(k) bid has to be specific enough for the lender and consultant to approve. We provide itemized line items for labor and materials that match the consultant’s work write-up, identify which items require permits from the Building Division, and include occupancy-inspection items so the home will be ready when the work is complete.

After closing, funds are released in draws as work progresses and is inspected. We submit each draw with photographs, a description of completed work and lien waivers from the trades involved. Change orders, which are common in older brick homes when walls are opened, are documented and submitted for approval before the additional work proceeds.

Because many 203(k) buyers are paying rent elsewhere while the work happens, our field manager keeps the schedule moving and communicates regularly with the buyer, the agent and the lender. Each party sees the same milestones, photos and paperwork, so nobody is working from an outdated picture of the job.

faqs.q: Can I buy a two-family flat with a 203(k) loan?
faqs.a: Yes, if you will occupy one of the units and the property and scope qualify. Flats are a popular 203(k) choice in St. Louis because rent from the second unit helps with the payment. The renovation must address both units as needed and meet FHA standards, and we prepare a bid that covers both apartments and building-wide items such as the roof and stacks.

faqs.q: Will masonry repairs push me into a Standard 203(k)?
faqs.a: Possibly. Tuckpointing alone may fit a Limited loan, but rebuilding parapets, replacing lintels or repairing structural walls is generally treated as structural work requiring the Standard program and a HUD consultant. We evaluate the masonry during our review so the loan type matches the work from the beginning, avoiding delays later. Your loan officer makes the final call on program fit.

faqs.q: Do you coordinate with my 203(k) consultant?
faqs.a: Yes. On Standard 203(k) loans, we work from the consultant’s work write-up, align our bid with it, and coordinate inspections and draw requests. The consultant and lender keep their oversight roles, and we serve as the contractor who prices, schedules and performs the work and submits draw documentation. Questions about change orders go through the consultant before any added work proceeds.

reo-renovation.title: REO Renovation Contractor in St. Louis, MO | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO and bank-owned renovations in St. Louis for servicers, banks and GSEs: vacant brick buildings, code compliance, occupancy readiness, reporting.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Renovations in St. Louis
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned and servicer-held properties in St. Louis present conditions that frame-house markets rarely see: brick walls missing courses after salvage theft, parapets collapsing into roofs, cast-iron stacks cracked by freezing and plaster soaked through by box-gutter leaks. Servicers, banks, REITs and Government-Sponsored Enterprises need a contractor that can assess these buildings honestly, document them thoroughly and bring them to a marketable standard. Genstone Construction is a preferred contractor for GSEs, with an executive team experienced in REO work. In St. Louis, one designated field manager coordinates licensed local contractors, handles permits and occupancy requirements and provides institutional-grade reporting, while Genstone Field Services supports preservation, inspections and code compliance on the same properties.

sections.h2: Conditions in vacant St. Louis properties
sections.body:
A vacant St. Louis house deteriorates in a predictable sequence. A failed roof or box gutter lets water into the top floor, plaster ceilings come down, floor framing begins to rot and the masonry absorbs moisture that freezes and pushes brick apart. Without heat, supply lines and radiators split in the first hard freeze.

On the north side and in some south city pockets, vacant buildings also face scrapping of copper and HVAC equipment, broken windows, squatting and fire. Brick theft is a distinct St. Louis problem: salvagers remove brick from walls, leaving buildings unstable and sometimes beyond repair.

We document each property’s condition with photographs and clear descriptions, separating immediate safety and securing work from repairs needed for marketability. That gives asset managers the information to decide whether to repair, sell as-is or pursue another disposition. Where a roof is open, temporary weather protection is usually the first recommendation.

The City of St. Louis Building Division can condemn unsafe buildings, and code enforcement follows complaints about open structures, debris and overgrowth. The Land Reutilization Authority holds a large number of vacant city-owned parcels, and neighbors on blocks with high vacancy are quick to report problems. For servicers, an unaddressed violation can lead to fines, emergency board-up charges or demolition orders that reduce recovery.

Genstone and Genstone Field Services help keep properties compliant: securing openings, clearing debris, maintaining exteriors and responding to notices with documented corrective work. When repairs require permits, we pull them and schedule inspections so the violation can be closed.

In St. Louis County, each municipality runs its own code enforcement and often its own occupancy inspection, and we track those requirements by address so the right repairs are completed before a property is listed or transferred. Notices are logged with dates, responses and photographs of the corrected conditions.

sections.h2: Repair options and reporting for servicers
sections.body:
We offer asset managers several repair levels rather than a single recommendation. A safe-and-secure package stabilizes the building, a marketable package addresses roof, masonry, mechanicals and occupancy-inspection items so more buyers can finance the property, and a fuller renovation applies where neighborhood comps support it, typically in south city bungalow neighborhoods with owner-occupant demand.

Each option is priced with labor, materials and a draw schedule, with dumpster and debris costs included. We provide before, during and after photographs, milestone reports and lien waivers formatted for servicer and GSE reporting, and final billing follows completion and approval.

For portfolios with multiple St. Louis properties, a single field manager coordinates each address, keeps reporting consistent and helps asset managers prioritize properties that are at risk of further deterioration or code enforcement action during the cold months. Freeze-sensitive properties are flagged before the first hard frost so winterization can be confirmed in time.

faqs.q: Can you stabilize a brick building with structural damage?
faqs.a: Often, yes. We coordinate structural assessment, shoring, roof repairs and masonry rebuilding where a building can be saved economically. Where the damage is too extensive, we document conditions clearly so the asset manager can consider sale or demolition. In St. Louis, salvaged brick and collapsed roofs are common factors in that evaluation, and an engineer’s opinion is often part of the file.

faqs.q: Do you prepare REO properties for occupancy inspections?
faqs.a: Yes. Many sales in the City of St. Louis and in county municipalities involve occupancy or point-of-sale inspections. We scope the required repairs, such as detectors, handrails, electrical hazards, plumbing leaks and paint condition, and complete them before listing or transfer. This helps avoid delays at closing and widens the pool of buyers, including those using FHA financing on entry-level homes.

faqs.q: Who do you work with on REO assignments?
faqs.a: Genstone works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, for which we are a preferred contractor. Our reporting, photo documentation and lien waiver practices are built for institutional requirements, and we coordinate multiple properties across St. Louis and the surrounding county through one field manager who knows each file, its history and its open items at any given time.
